:::: {#sets .learning-object concept-id="urn:example:concept:sets" revision="sets-2" label="Sets" context="elementary-maths" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
## Sets {#sets-title}

**Objective:** Read a membership statement for a specified finite set.

**Quick check:** If $A=\{1,2\}$, which of $1\in A$ and $3\in A$ holds?
Explain your choice before consulting an explanation.

::: {.learning-view level="introductory" revision="sets-intro-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
A set is a collection of objects. We write $x \in A$ when $x$ belongs to $A$.
For example, $A=\{1,2\}$ contains two elements.
:::

::: {.learning-view level="advanced" revision="sets-advanced-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
Here sets are used in ordinary elementary mathematics. Membership is denoted
by $\in$, and $A\subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ is an element of $B$.
No foundational axiom system is supplied by this example.
:::
::::

:::: {#functions .learning-object concept-id="urn:example:concept:functions" revision="functions-2" label="Functions" context="elementary-maths" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
## Functions {#functions-title}

**Objective:** Identify the domain, codomain and output of a specified function.

**Quick check:** For $f:\{1,2\}\to\{2,4\}$ with $f(x)=2x$, state the
domain, codomain and value of $f(2)$.

::: {.learning-view level="introductory" revision="functions-intro-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
A function $f:A\to B$ assigns exactly one element of $B$ to each element of $A$.
For example, $f:\{1,2\}\to\{2,4\}$ with $f(x)=2x$ is a function.
Review [sets](#sets) if the domain and codomain are unfamiliar.
:::

::: {.learning-view level="advanced" revision="functions-advanced-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
A function $f:A\to B$ is a total, single-valued relation from $A$ to $B$:
for every $a\in A$ there exists exactly one $b\in B$ with $(a,b)\in f$.
Its domain and codomain are part of the specified function.
:::

:::: {#proofs .learning-object concept-id="urn:example:concept:proof-patterns" revision="proofs-2" label="Proof patterns" context="elementary-maths" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
## Proof patterns {#proofs-title}

**Objective:** Distinguish a universal justification from a few supporting examples.

**Quick check:** Why would checking two integers usually be insufficient to prove
a statement about every integer? What could a single counterexample establish?

::: {.learning-view level="introductory" revision="proofs-intro-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
To prove a statement holds for every element, start with an arbitrary element
and justify the required conclusion. A worked example alone does not prove
a statement about every element.
:::

::: {.learning-view level="advanced" revision="proofs-advanced-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
For universal introduction, choose an arbitrary element satisfying the stated
domain assumptions and derive the predicate without additional restrictions
on that element. This is pedagogical preparation, not a formal proof checker.
:::
::::

:::: {#bijections .learning-object concept-id="urn:example:concept:bijections" revision="bijections-2" label="Bijections" context="elementary-maths" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
## Bijections {#bijections-title}

::: {#bijections-task}
**Objective:** Determine whether a specified function is bijective by checking
injectivity and surjectivity against its stated domain and codomain.

**Shared task and assumptions:** Work with the finite sets $A=\{1,2\}$ and
$B=\{2,4\}$ and the function $f:A\to B$ defined by $f(x)=2x$.
Justify whether $f$ is injective and whether it is surjective. Try to give your
own reasons before reading a hint or the solution. Both explanation levels below
support this same task; switching levels does not change these assumptions.

**Transfer question:** Now define $g:A\to C$ by $g(x)=2x$, where
$C=\{2,4,6\}$. The domain and rule are retained, but the codomain has changed.
Which properties does $g$ have? Explain why a claim about $f$ cannot simply be
transferred to $g$ without checking the specified codomain.
:::

::: {.learning-view level="introductory" revision="bijections-intro-2" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
A bijection $f:A\to B$ pairs the elements of $A$ and $B$ one to one:
different inputs have different outputs, and every element of $B$ is reached.
:::

::: {.learning-view level="advanced" revision="bijections-advanced-1" review="author-reviewed" reviewed-by="Example fixture declaration"}
A bijection $f:A\to B$ is injective and surjective:
$f(a)=f(a')\Rightarrow a=a'$ for $a,a'\in A$, and
$\forall b\in B\,\exists a\in A\;(f(a)=b)$.
The domain and codomain, including the quantifiers above, remain fixed across views.
:::

::: {#bijections-hint-1 .callout-tip}
## Hint 1: Check the two conditions separately

Injectivity asks whether different inputs can produce the same output.
Surjectivity asks whether every element of the specified codomain is produced.
List the outputs, then compare them with the codomain in each question.
:::

::: {#bijections-hint-2 .callout-tip}
## Hint 2: Look for an unreached element

Both rules produce $2$ from input $1$ and $4$ from input $2$.
For the transfer question, is every element of $C$ in that list? Can an input
outside the specified domain be used to satisfy the condition?
:::

::: {#bijections-solution .callout-note}
## Explained solution and misconception check

The function $f$ is injective: for $a,a'\in A$, the equality $f(a)=f(a')$
gives $2a=2a'$, hence $a=a'$. It is also surjective onto $B$: the element
$2$ has preimage $1$, and the element $4$ has preimage $2$. Thus $f$ is bijective.

The same injectivity argument applies to $g$. However, $g$ is not surjective
onto $C$, because $6\in C$ has no preimage in $A=\{1,2\}$. Choosing $3$
would not help: $3\notin A$. Therefore $g$ is injective but not bijective.

A common mistaken claim is that the formula $2x$ alone determines whether a
function is bijective. This pair is a counterexample: the specified domain and
codomain matter. Describing $g$ as “surjective onto its image” uses the image
$\{2,4\}$ in place of $C$ and does not establish surjectivity onto its stated
codomain.

or mark an answer correct.
